newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Red Cross seeks medicine, more food for N. Korea.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross seeks medicine, more food for N. Korea.

text.p: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies appealed on Thursday for 26 million Swiss francs ($18 million) to increase its food aid and start providing medical care in famine-threatened North Korea.
The world's largest humanitarian network presented the appeal at a two-day donors meeting attended by officials from 15 member societies, including those of North and South Korea.
Under its expanded relief operation, due to begin in July, the IFRC will quintuple its food aid programme, now supplying rations to 139,000 flood victims, to cover 700,000 people.
A one-year public health programme to provide medicines and equipment to clinics and hospitals, and train first aid workers, is to be funded, according to a Federation statement.
The appeal will also support a three-year disaster preparedness programme to stock emergency supplies, improve communications and training in evacuation and rescue techniques.

"The expanded operation will allow a much greater number of people to receive adequate food rations until the next harvest, in late October, and will give some 2.6 million people in 19 counties access to better health care," said George Weber, secretary-general of the world relief body.

Weber signed the appeal document at a ceremony in Geneva attended by Paik Yong Ho, secretary-general of the North Korean Red Cross, and Kim Heh nam, head of international relations at South Korea's Red Cross.
Officials from the Red Cross societies of the United States, Britain, France, Germany, China and Japan are among those taking part in the donors meeting in Geneva.
Spokeswoman Marie-Francoise Borel told Reuters: "We plan to feed 700,000 people until late October or November to make sure they are tided over until the next harvest.
"We will make a new assessment after the harvest," she added. "Obviously, we are praying there are no floods this year.
IFRC, working close with the North Korean Red Cross, began its relief programme in November 1995 after devastating floods destroyed homes, food stocks and arable land.
Some 500,000 people were left destitute, suffering severe food shortages and the crisis was compounded by floods in 1996.
"Public food distribution has been reduced to 100-150 grams per person per day and most warehouses are empty," IFRC said.
"A Federation assessment team who visited North Korea in mid-May saw malnourished and sick children and said people were cooking roots and tree bark to supplement their diet," it added.
IFRC's previous appeal of 13.5 million Swiss francs (nearly $9 million), issued last November, has been fully funded.

Under the first direct pact between the Red Cross societies of rival North and South in more than a decade, representatives signed an agreement in Beijing on May 26 on the delivery of some 50,000 tonnes of food, mainly corn, from Seoul to Pyongyang.
The South Korean organisation has delivered 11,200 tonnes of corn to North Korea via China in the past week as part of its promise to donate 50,000 tonnes of food by the end of July.

In Seoul, Rhee Jong-geun, a spokesman for the South Korean Red Cross, said Pyongyang complained by telephone on Monday that the corn had dead rats, twigs and lime powder in it. He said the corn was bought in China by South Korean civic groups.

"The North said some of the packages were lighter than marked, contained dangerous levels of lime powder, chunks of dirt, stones, twigs and dead rats," said Rhee. "They asked that more attention be paid to prevent such an occurrence."

The Korea Sharing Movement, which is campaigning in South Korea to raise funds to aid the North, said Chinese companies that sold the corn had apologised for "making packaging mistakes" and agreed to make compensation.
